resources.string: Scans the screen to find targetable elements and perform tasks according to the specified rules.
Enable the agent to be able to scan screen contents and run automations
TapOk lets you automate taps and other actions in Android apps.
Follow this quick tutorial to learn how to set up your first automation.
TapOk requires a background service to scan the screen and run your automations.
, find TapOk (it may be under \"Installed apps\" or \"Downloaded services\") and switch it on.
Once enabled, a floating button will appear on your screen. You\'ll use it in the next step.
To write an automation you need to know what screen elements TapOk can interact with. A screen scanner is provided to help with that.
"Open the app you want to automate, then tap "
" on TapOk's floating button to capture a scan of the active window."
, then \"View scans\" on the floating button and open your recent scan.
Elements that TapOk can interact with will be highlighted. Tap the element you want to automate, such as a button, to view its data.

Look for a property that uniquely identifies it. View ID is the most reliable, but if it\'s empty, you can use a combination of package name and text or any other listed property that sets the element apart. Copy or save these values for the next step.
Switch to the Rules tab and create a new rule.
Fill in the values you got on the previous step, choose an action and save the rule.
That\'s it! TapOk will now automatically trigger that action whenever it sees an element matching your description.
To automate your actions, TapOk uses the Accessibility API:
analyzes the active window\'s contents and identifies targetable elements
performs clicks and gestures on your behalf according to rules you specify
The data is processed within TapOk, locally on your device. It is not transmitted to external servers or third parties.
Select a rule to edit, or create a new one
The rule\'s action runs on any UI element that matches all the following criteria.
One of these is used to find a matching element. If multiple are filled in, the topmost one is used for the search and the rest act as post-search filters.
After the search, these filters are applied. Only fill in when needed to distinguish between similar elements — additional filters slow down matching.
The action performed on the matched element. If multiple elements match simultaneously, the action may run only on some of them.
Name of the rule for your own reference.
\"Package name\" of the window\'s top-level element — normally the owning app\'s package. Visible in the top bar when viewing a scan.
An element matches if its \"View ID\" is exactly this value.

An element matches if this text appears as a substring of its \"Content description\" or \"Text\", case-insensitive. \"Text\" is usually only searched when the element\'s \"Class name\" is \"android.widget.TextView\".
An element matches if its \"Package name\" is exactly this value. Usually the same as the window-level package, so should typically be left empty.
An element matches if its \"Class name\" is exactly this value.
